observed.reply:
In **Chapter 9** of *The Adventures of Pinocchio*, Pinocchio tells himself: “Today I’ll follow the pipes, and tomorrow I’ll go to school. There’s
always plenty of time to go to school,”

The useful resemblance isn’t that your situation makes you “a terrible person.” It’s the structure of the bargain: a real future intention is used to make a present choice feel harmless. Your wish to repay your sister may be sincere, while still not being enough to protect the study evenings she is giving you.

So perhaps the gap to examine is between **gratitude and follow-through**: not “Am I good or bad?” but “What am I doing with the help I’ve been given, and what small boundary would make tonight different?” You could treat her support as something to honor in the present, not only something to repay after you qualify.

What usually pulls you away when one of those study evenings begins—the task itself, the pressure attached to qualifying, or the ease of choosing something more immediately rewarding?

evidence.text:
See Pinocchio hurrying off to school with his new A-B-C book under
his arm! As he walked along, his brain was busy planning hundreds of
wonderful things, building hundreds of castles in the air. Talking to
himself, he said:

“In school today, I’ll learn to read, tomorrow to write, and the day
after tomorrow I’ll do arithmetic. Then, clever as I am, I can earn a
lot of money. With the very first pennies I make, I’ll buy Father a new
cloth coat. Cloth, did I say? No, it shall be of gold and silver with
diamond buttons. That poor man certainly deserves it; for, after all,
isn’t he in his shirt sleeves because he was good enough to buy a
book for me? On this cold day, too! Fathers are indeed good to their
children!”

As he talked to himself, he thought he heard sounds of pipes and drums
coming from a distance: pi-pi-pi, pi-pi-pi. . .zum, zum, zum, zum.

He stopped to listen. Those sounds came from a little street that led to
a small village along the shore.

“What can that noise be? What a nuisance that I have to go to school!
Otherwise. . .”

There he stopped, very much puzzled. He felt he had to make up his mind
for either one thing or another. Should he go to school, or should he
follow the pipes?

“Today I’ll follow the pipes, and tomorrow I’ll go to school. There’s
always plenty of time to go to school,” decided the little rascal at
last, shrugging his shoulders.

No sooner said than done. He started down the street, going like the
wind. On he ran, and louder grew the sounds of pipe and drum: pi-pi-pi,
pi-pi-pi, pi-pi-pi . . .zum, zum, zum, zum.

Suddenly, he found himself in a large square, full of people standing in
front of a little wooden building painted in brilliant colors.

“What is that house?” Pinocchio asked a little boy near him.

“Read the sign and you’ll know.”

“I’d like to read, but somehow I can’t today.”

observed.reply:
Try this one small promise for this week: **take back one specific chore your sister has been covering, and tell her why.** For example: “I really notice that you’re making room for this course by handling ____. I’m going to take that one back this week—thank you for giving me the chance to study.”

Then make the next study evening very small: commit to just **20 minutes**, with the materials ready beforehand. If you miss it, the conclusion is not “I'm a terrible person”; it’s simply “that plan didn’t happen, so I can reset and try the next small step.” Honouring her help can mean responding honestly and continuing—not proving that you never struggle.

Which single chore would feel concrete but still manageable to take back this week?

In Chapter 9, Pinocchio tells himself:

“Today I’ll follow the pipes, and tomorrow I’ll go to school. There’s
always plenty of time to go to school,” decided the little rascal at
last, shrugging his shoulders.

The gap you’re describing doesn’t require the verdict “I’m a terrible person.” It may be more useful to separate three things: you genuinely value your sister’s help, you imagine a future way of repaying it, and the study evenings available now keep getting spent elsewhere. The future intention matters, but it can also make the present choice feel less urgent.

You might ask, without self-condemnation: **What would make the next study evening concrete enough that I don’t have to rely on the future version of me who has already qualified?** Even one small, defined block would turn repayment from a distant promise into something you’re beginning now.

“Today I’ll follow the pipes, and tomorrow I’ll go to school. There’s
always plenty of time to go to school,” decided the little rascal at
last, shrugging his shoulders.

“What do you care about school? You can go there tomorrow. With a lesson
more or less, we are always the same donkeys.”

“Very well, then. Let’s see who gets there first!” cried Pinocchio.

At the signal, the little troop, with books under their arms, dashed
across the fields. Pinocchio led the way, running as if on wings, the
others following as fast as they could.

What was his surprise and his joy when, on looking himself over, he saw
that he was no longer a Marionette, but that he had become a real live
boy!
